hints: Think about what you see when a Group 2 metal compound is heated strongly on a nichrome wire in a blue Bunsen flame.
Recall the characteristic brick red colour for calcium compounds and the pale green colour for barium compounds.
walkthrough:
Picture the flame test in the lab**
You clean a wire, dip it in the solid, and hold it in the edge of a blue flame. The heat excites the metal ions and they give out light of a very specific colour as the electrons fall back down. Each Group 2 metal has its own fingerprint colour.

Fix the two colours in memory**
Calcium always gives a red flame, often described as brick red or orange red. Barium always gives a green flame, often described as pale green or apple green. Learn them as a pair: calcium red, barium green.

Final answer: calcium: red (brick red / orange red) flame
barium: green (pale / apple green) flame

hints: Recall the decomposition equation $\text{MCO}_{3}(\text{s}) \rightarrow \text{MO}(\text{s}) + \text{CO}_{2}(\text{g})$ and think about whether more or less heating is needed from calcium to barium.
Compare the size of $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ and think about how ionic radius affects charge density and polarising power.
Think about how a small highly polarising cation distorts the $\text{CO}_{3}^{2-}$ ion and weakens a C-O bond, making decomposition easier.
walkthrough:
See the trend in stability**
Write the reaction: $$\text{MCO}_{3}(\text{s}) \rightarrow \text{MO}(\text{s}) + \text{CO}_{2}(\text{g})$$ Going down Group 2 from calcium to barium, the carbonate becomes harder to break down. You have to heat barium carbonate much more strongly to get it to release $\text{CO}_{2}$. So decomposition temperature increases down the group.

Connect size to pulling power**
All the ions here are $2+$, so the charge is the same. What changes is size. $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ is small, $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ is much larger because it has extra electron shells. A small ion packs the same $2+$ charge into a tiny volume, so it has high charge density and high polarising power. A large ion has low charge density and low polarising power.

See what polarisation does to carbonate**
Picture the $\text{CO}_{3}^{2-}$ ion sitting next to $\text{M}^{2+}$. A small $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ pulls strongly on the electron cloud of the carbonate oxygen atoms. It distorts the $\text{CO}_{3}^{2-}$ ion and weakens one of the C-O bonds, almost pulling it towards $\text{CO}_{2}$ plus $\text{O}^{2-}$. That makes decomposition easy. A large $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ distorts the anion much less, the C-O bonds stay stronger, and you need more thermal energy to force the breakdown.

Final answer: The temperature needed for decomposition increases down Group 2.
Down the group ionic radius increases so charge density and polarising power of $\text{M}^{2+}$ decreases.
There is less distortion / polarisation and less weakening of the bonds in the $\text{CO}_{3}^{2-}$ ion, so the carbonate is more thermally stable.

hints: Think about the appearance of the gas evolved, $\text{CO}_{2}$, and whether you would be able to see it in air.
Compare the colour and state of the starting carbonate and the oxide formed, for example white $\text{MCO}_{3}$ to white $\text{MO}$.
walkthrough:
Look for the gas**
The only gas made is $$\text{MCO}_{3}(\text{s}) \rightarrow \text{MO}(\text{s}) + \text{CO}_{2}(\text{g})$$ Carbon dioxide is completely colourless. It looks just like air, so even if decomposition is happening you see no smoke, no brown fumes, no coloured gas.

Look at the solid**
Both the Group 2 carbonate and the Group 2 oxide are white solids. You start with a white powder and you end with a white powder. With no colour change and no visible gas, it is very hard to tell by eye that a reaction has occurred.

Final answer: The evolved $\text{CO}_{2}$ is colourless and invisible in air, so no fumes or colour change in the gas is seen.
The solid changes from one white solid ($\text{MCO}_{3}$) to another white solid ($\text{MO}$), so no visible change in the solid is seen.
